newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: World Bank closes Bangladesh jute credit project.
newsitem.headline: World Bank closes Bangladesh jute credit project.

text.p: The World Bank has ended a credit programme for Bangladesh's jute sector after Dhaka failed to streamline production of the fibre along lines outlined in a 1994 agreement, World Bank officials said on Friday.

"The $250 million credit programme had met its natural death. The deadline for disbursing the credit expired on June 30, 1997," said Alfredo Dammert, the World Bank's senior Private Sector Development Specialist for South Asia Region.
"The programme will not continue, and we are not able to support this particular programme," he told Reuters on Friday.

The Jute Sector Adjustment Credit (JSAC) agreement was signed between the International Development Association (IDA), a soft-loan subsidiary of the World Bank, and the Bangladesh government in February 1994.

Conditions it entailed included "elimination of excess capacity (looms) in the jute industry by closing nine of the 29 public sector mills and downsizing two large public mills; retrenchment of about 20,000 employees in the state-run mills; privatisation of 18 public mills; and re-training for retrenched workers under a social safety net progaramme."
The government, however, only shut down four public sector jute mills, downsized one, shed about 12,000 workers and abolished the state-run Bangladesh Jute Corporation.
Those measures were not enough for the World Bank.

"We feel sorry that the present government has failed to implement its commitments in the jute sector," said Owaise Saadat, chief of the World Bank's Private Sector Development & Finance Unit in Bangladesh.
"The World Bank made an overall assessment of progress under the JSAC in early June," he said.
The bank disbursed $50 million in a first instalment in April 1994. But remaining instalments were suspended.

The World Bank extended by six months the deadline for disbursing the rest of the soft credit, effective from January 1, 1997, after the government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina requested a one-year extension.
By failing to meet the bank's preconditions for the programme, Bangladesh lost the chance for another extension to the deadline, World Bank officials said.
The government spends about $500 million annually on subsidies to state-owned jute and other companies, government officials said.

"The jute sector's contribution in the economy is not very significant nowadays, although it has an important role in (our) socio-political life," said Mohammad Abdul Hannan, Secretary in the Ministry of Jute.

"As such, we are also not insisting on (continuing) this particular (JSAC) credit programme. What we now need is a modernisation programme for the (jute) sector. We need technical assistance from the World Bank," he told Reuters.
Other ministry officials said the government has repeatedly called for a tender to sell the loss-making jute mills but the response was disappointing.
"For example, one buyer offered only 80 million taka ($1.83 million) for Karim Jute Mill whereas the real price of the mill was 1.164 billion taka ($200 million)," one official said.
"We can't throw public assets into the water," he said.
Jute, a plant fibre used for sackings, mats and cord, is the world's second most consumed fibre after cotton. The world's major jute producers are Pakistan, India and China.

Bangladesh's jute industry is facing hard times, partly due to tough competition from cheaper, more durable synthetics and a growing reluctance among local farmers to continue production following a rise in the cost of manufacturing the fibre.
As a result, Bangladesh's jute exports have slowly tapered in recent years.
The World Bank's Dammert, however, said the bank would continue to support other Bangladesh reforms. "Still we are committed to support the government in other reforms," he said.
